title: Building a CMMS That People Actually Use
excerpt: Most CMMS implementations fail not because the software is wrong, but because the structure is wrong. Here is what separates a system that gets adopted from one that gets ignored.
content:
In my experience across multiple CMMS deployments, the most common failure mode is not a technical one. The software works. The modules are configured. The licenses are paid for.

And yet — six months later — technicians are still using whiteboards and spreadsheets. The CMMS is technically live, but operationally dead.

## Why CMMS Implementations Fail

The short answer: the system was built for management, not for the people who have to use it every day.

When a CMMS is implemented top-down — designed primarily to produce KPI reports for leadership — it becomes a reporting burden rather than a working tool. Technicians feel like they are doing data entry for someone else's dashboard. Compliance drops. The system stops reflecting reality. And once the data is unreliable, the whole investment collapses.

## The Principle That Changes Everything

Design the system from the field up, not the boardroom down.

This means starting with one question: *What does a technician need to do their job better today?* If the CMMS can answer that question — give them clear work orders, the right parts information, access to equipment history — then adoption follows naturally. The KPI dashboards become a byproduct of a system that is genuinely useful, not a burden layered on top of it.

## Three Structural Decisions That Determine Adoption

**1. Work order clarity**

A work order should tell a technician exactly what needs to be done, where, with what tools, and what the expected outcome looks like. Vague work orders ('check equipment') create ambiguity, and ambiguity creates workarounds. Workarounds mean the data is wrong.

**2. Asset hierarchy that matches reality**

If your functional location structure does not reflect how technicians actually navigate the plant, they will never find what they are looking for. The hierarchy should mirror the physical reality of the facility — not an org chart, not an accountant's asset register.

**3. Minimal but mandatory fields**

Every mandatory field that is not genuinely useful is a reason to abandon the system. Audit your required fields ruthlessly. If you cannot explain why a piece of data is captured and how it improves decisions, remove the requirement.

## The Long Game

A well-adopted CMMS is one of the highest-leverage investments a maintenance organization can make. The data it generates — equipment history, failure patterns, cost trends — compounds in value over time. But only if the data is accurate. And the data is only accurate if people use the system.

Build for the technician first. Everything else follows.

title: What Reactive Maintenance Is Really Costing You
excerpt: The true cost of reactive maintenance is never just the repair. Here is how to calculate the full impact and make the business case for a proactive strategy.
content:
Every maintenance manager knows that reactive maintenance is expensive. But most organizations significantly underestimate *how* expensive — because they only count the visible costs.

## The Visible Costs

When a pump fails unexpectedly, the visible costs are clear: the parts, the labour, the contractor call-out fee. Management sees these on the work order and categorizes them as maintenance spend.

In most plants, this number is already 2–3x what the equivalent planned maintenance would have cost.

## The Hidden Costs

But the visible costs are usually the smaller portion. The real damage comes from:

**Production loss.** Unplanned downtime during a critical production window can cost more in a single day than the entire annual maintenance budget for that asset. In oil and gas, an unplanned shutdown of a key compressor can mean tens of thousands of dollars per hour in lost throughput.

**Safety and environmental risk.** Equipment that fails unexpectedly creates conditions that planned maintenance would have prevented. The liability exposure from a single incident dwarfs any savings from deferred maintenance.

**Secondary damage.** A bearing that fails because it was not lubricated on schedule can destroy a shaft, a housing, and adjacent components. The $40 lubrication task becomes a $40,000 overhaul.

**Expedited parts and logistics.** Emergency parts procurement at premium pricing, expedited freight, and after-hours contractor rates routinely add 40–60% to the direct material and labour cost.

## Building the Business Case

To make the case for a proactive maintenance program, calculate the *true* cost of your top ten reactive failures from the past twelve months. Include:

- Direct repair cost
- Production loss (hours × throughput rate)
- Secondary damage
- Expedited procurement premium
- Overtime and call-out premiums

In every analysis I have done, this number is large enough to fund a comprehensive preventive maintenance program many times over.

**The numbers make the case.** Your job is to surface them.

title: The Asset Register Is Your Foundation — Don't Skip It
excerpt: A clean, accurate asset register is the unglamorous work that everything else depends on. Here is why most organizations skip it and how to do it right.
content:
When organizations implement a CMMS, there is always pressure to get to the 'real work' quickly — to start issuing work orders, running PM schedules, generating reports. The asset register feels like a prerequisite to tick off rather than a strategic investment.

This is the single most expensive mistake in CMMS implementation.

## What an Asset Register Actually Is

An asset register is not just a list of equipment. It is a structured record that links every maintainable asset to its location, specifications, maintenance history, criticality rating, spare parts, and associated documentation.

When it is built correctly, every question a maintenance professional needs to answer starts with the asset register: What do we have? Where is it? What condition is it in? What are the failure modes? What parts do we need to maintain it?

## Why Organizations Skip the Work

Building a proper asset register is slow and not glamorous. It requires walking the plant, verifying nameplate data, cross-referencing drawings, and resolving years of inconsistent naming conventions. For a mid-sized facility, this can take weeks.

It is also invisible to leadership. Nobody reports to the board that the functional location hierarchy is clean. The pressure is always toward visible outputs.

## The Cost of a Poor Asset Register

A CMMS built on an incomplete or inaccurate asset register produces unreliable data from day one. Maintenance plans are applied to the wrong equipment. Spare parts are ordered for assets that no longer exist. KPIs are calculated against a population that does not reflect reality.

You cannot build a reliable maintenance program on an unreliable foundation.

## How to Do It Right

Allocate real time and resources to the asset register before you go live. For each asset:

1. Verify the physical location and functional location code
2. Capture nameplate data (manufacturer, model, serial number, installation date)
3. Assign a criticality rating (A/B/C or equivalent)
4. Link to relevant drawings and manuals
5. Document known failure history

Then — critically — establish a governance process to keep it current. An asset register that was accurate on go-live and has not been maintained is just as dangerous as one that was never built.

Do the unglamorous work. It is what everything else depends on.
